Some good comments there. I'm on the traveling is overrated bus myself - and have taken some flack for that, but then I hate air travel. It's interesting to see exceptionally well traveled people argue the other side though. Though honestly there are many places I just have little desire to go. And I am particularly enamored with my own country. Life is short and it takes a long time just to see all of America. But there are some places I'd rather visit multiple times than some other places even once.

I do notice the strongly pro-traveling types tend to place it in importance above, say, reading in terms of quality of experience. There I really disagree. Travel mostly provides some pretty superficial experiences. A lot of really well traveled people I've encountered are even businessmen who have little time to read and would even have little time to travel if it wasn't part of their job.

For some it is, for others it's not.

For me, it's about gaining perspective and helping to understand things that are lost in translation when read or seen through media.

The big picture I gained is that North America is a relative cultural wasteland, especially Canada, Mexico is a bigger shithole than I expected, South America is nicer than I expected, Africa is hopeless and Europe truly is the holy land.

Vis-a-vis Europe vs. North America did you really need to travel to gain such insights though? Europe has more culture by virtue of being older. I find England rather suffocating through lack of space. This is an issue affecting Western Europe more broadly. All the castles are even somewhat alien. And don't get me started on the prices...

But then I'm a bit of a modernist, if maybe a reactionary modernis, and an American with a preference for wide open spaces.

My larger issue though is that traveling is mostly ancillary to real study. A guy won't learn anything comprehensive about a nation's history, politics, or even culture simply by traveling there. It mostly helps get a feel for things with add-ons through anecdotal experiences. I guess if one puts a lot of emphasis on the hustle and bustle that is Bangkok or things smelling food is very important this may ring untrue though.

I was lucky that a lot of my travel involved doing business, which allowed me to get more immersed into local cultures. One thing to go to a place, enjoy some food and maybe visit a museum or a sacred site and then move on... another is having to deal with locals, which requires deeper immersion into their world and helps understanding how they see things. As such it's not "better" than reading a book. It's different, complementary, providing you with knowledge that is difficult to communicate through an indirect medium. That is what I compared to things being lost in translation.

My cultural wasteland comment was meant in a broader sense. Yes, Europe is older and has more heritage "items". But the various people there have stronger sense of identity and connection to history. This kind of attitude is pervasive and when I criticize it, the locals look at me like I am from another planet. It's nice to have books (that most people don't read) and photos of memories posted on Facebook, but to create continuity, you need lasting physical symbols. In Europe, historical architecture is a big part of that. In North America, what matters is new, global and replaceable.
